title: Yellow skin, abdominal pain and fever in a 56-year-old accountant
desc: This station involves a focused jaundice history and examination of a 56-year-old woman in general practice. She has had 5 days of jaundice with right upper quadrant pain, fever, pale stools, itch, dizziness and new confusion, on a background of known untreated gallstones. The candidate then interprets her worsening observations, blood results, ultrasound and next-day ERCP report. They recognise severe acute cholangitis from common bile duct stones with sepsis, hypotension and hypoperfusion (at risk of septic shock), and plan sepsis resuscitation, urgent biliary drainage, cholecystectomy and safety netting.
focus: Taking a jaundice history that recognises Charcot's triad and confusion, and managing severe acute cholangitis from choledocholithiasis
diagnosis: Sepsis with hypotension (at risk of septic shock)
stem: You are a fourth-year medical student on your general practice rotation. Michelle Stark, a 56-year-old woman, has come to the practice because her skin has turned yellow. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first. A practice nurse is available.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ms Stark and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Ms Stark's observations, blood results, ultrasound report and ERCP report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Michelle Stark, a 56-year-old accountant. You feel unwell and hot. You are a little slow to answer and now and then lose your train of thought, but you can give your history. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate decides in Part 1 that you need hospital, the examiner says the supervising GP agrees and is arranging it, and the station carries on.

Opening line: “I've just noticed that I look a bit yellow.”

The yellow colour (give only when asked):

  • Your skin and the whites of your eyes are the most yellow.
  • You noticed it about 5 days ago. It has been there all the time since then, and it started around the same time as your other symptoms.
  • It has never happened before.
  • You haven't tried anything for it, and nothing makes it worse.

Other symptoms (give only when asked):

  • Tummy pain: across your upper tummy, worst on the right under the ribs, 6 out of 10. It started around the same time as the yellow colour and is there most of the time. It doesn't go to your shoulder or back. It isn't related to meals. Nurofen hasn't helped.
  • Fever: you have felt hot and sweaty. You haven't taken your temperature.
  • Poo: pale, almost clay-coloured, for the past few days. It isn't greasy, and it isn't hard to flush.
  • Urine: “I haven't really noticed. I haven't been drinking much.”
  • Itch: you have been itchy all over and keep scratching.
  • Concentration: “I haven't been able to focus at work in the past week, and my co-worker said I seemed confused one day.” Only say this when asked about confusion, memory or concentration, or about anything else you've noticed. Don't describe it any further: you didn't really notice it yourself.
  • Dizziness: you have felt light-headed, mostly when you stand up, for the past couple of days. You haven't fainted or fallen.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Pain after fatty meals, indigestion or heartburn.
  • Shaking chills (rigors), pain in the tip of your shoulder, going off your food.
  • Feeling generally run down or achy in your muscles before this started, nausea or vomiting.
  • Weight loss, or greasy, floating poo.
  • Being yellow before, including when fasting or unwell; tiredness or breathlessness from anaemia; any blood disorder in the family; any new medicines.
  • Injecting drugs, tattoos, blood transfusions, new sexual partners, or contact with anyone who was yellow.

Past medical history:

  • Gallstones, found on a scan when you were 53. They never caused any symptoms and were never treated: “The doctor said to leave them alone.”
  • Overweight. Only if asked: “The nurse said my BMI was 32.”
  • No operations and no hospital admissions. No recent travel. Your immunisations are up to date.
  • Only if asked about your background: you are Caucasian.

Medications:

  • Nurofen (ibuprofen), 2 tablets a few times a day for the past few days, for the pain. It hasn't helped.
  • A daily multivitamin.
  • No other prescription, over-the-counter or herbal medicines.

Allergies: latex (you get an itchy rash from latex gloves). No medicine allergies.

Family history: your mother is overweight and has type 2 diabetes. Your father has COPD. You have no brothers or sisters and no children. No liver or blood diseases in the family.

Social history:

  • You smoked half a pack a day for 5 years in your 20s, and haven't smoked since.
  • Alcohol: a couple of drinks about twice a month.
  • You work as an accountant.
  • You don't exercise much, and you eat a lot of takeaway.
  • You live with your husband and your dog. Your husband and other family live in town.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: “Could it be gallstones? I've had that before.”
  • Concern: you are worried. Something is clearly wrong, and the trouble focusing scares you.
  • Expectation: you want to know what's going on and get it sorted.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: looks unwell, flushed and sweaty, and obviously jaundiced. Lying still on the couch. Weight 87 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 32.
  • Observations (10:20): temperature 38.6 °C, HR 112 regular, BP 104/66, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, capillary BGL 7.4 mmol/L, pain 6/10.
  • Conscious state: alert and knows where she is, but gives the wrong day of the week. Slow to answer. No asterixis. No focal neurological signs.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes, CRT 3 seconds, cool peripheries.
  • Skin and eyes: jaundiced skin, scleral icterus, scratch marks on her forearms and legs.
  • Hands: no clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema or Dupuytren's contracture.
  • Chest wall and face: no spider naevi. No xanthelasma.
  • Neck: no cervical or left supraclavicular (Virchow's) lymph nodes.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Heart sounds dual, tachycardic, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen, inspection: obese, not distended, no scars, no caput medusae.
  • Abdomen, palpation: tender in the right upper quadrant and the epigastrium, with voluntary guarding in the right upper quadrant. No rigidity or rebound. Murphy's sign negative. Liver edge not palpable below the costal margin. No palpable gallbladder. Spleen not palpable. No masses.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds present.
  • Renal angles: not tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Michelle's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language and responds with empathy to her worry. Notices that she seems slow and vague, and checks this tactfully rather than ignoring it.
History
Characterises the jaundice: skin and eyes, noticed 5 days ago, constant since, never had it before, nothing tried and nothing makes it worse.

Characterises the abdominal pain: diffuse upper abdominal pain, worst in the right upper quadrant, 6/10, started with the jaundice, no radiation to the shoulder or back, not linked to meals, no relief from Nurofen.
check.d: Award for site, onset, severity and radiation; other features optional.

check.x: Asks about the features of cholestasis (the 4 Ps: pee, poo, pruritus, pain):

kids.x: Stool colour: pale, clay-coloured stools.
Urine colour: she hasn't noticed a change.
Itch: generalised itch with scratching.

check.x: Asks about infection and sepsis:

kids.x: Fever: feels hot and sweaty, not measured; rigors (denied).
kids.d: Credit asking about rigors here or under 9.1.

kids.x: Confusion or poor concentration: draws out the trouble focusing at work and her co-worker's comment that she seemed confused.
kids.d: She only mentions this when asked about confusion, memory or concentration, or asked an open question about other symptoms.

kids.x: Dizziness: light-headed on standing for 2 days, no falls or fainting.

check.x: Asks about features that rule other causes of jaundice in or out:
check.d: Full marks for at least 3 associated symptoms from at least 3 of these differentials.

kids.x: Biliary colic or cholecystitis: pain after meals, dyspepsia, rigors, shoulder-tip pain, anorexia.
Acute hepatitis: viral risk factors (injecting drugs, tattoos, transfusions, sexual contacts, travel, jaundiced contacts), alcohol, malaise, vomiting, anorexia, myalgia or prodromal illness.
Pancreatic head tumour: weight loss, steatorrhoea.
Haemolysis or Gilbert's syndrome: previous jaundice (including with fasting or illness), symptoms of anaemia, family history, new medicines.

check.x: Takes the past medical history and identifies the known gallstones found at 53, asymptomatic and untreated.
check.d: Also credit BMI 32, no surgery or admissions, no travel, immunisations up to date (not required for the critical mark).

check.x: Takes a medication history: Nurofen several times a day for the past few days without benefit, and a multivitamin. No other prescription, over-the-counter or herbal medicines.
Asks about allergies: latex (rash), no medicine allergies.
check.d: Confirming she has no drug allergy matters for antibiotic choice; the latex allergy matters for latex-free equipment (gloves, catheter, endoscopy, theatre).

check.x: Takes a family history: mother obese with type 2 diabetes, father with COPD, no siblings or children, no liver or blood disease.

Takes a social history: smoked half a pack a day for 5 years in her 20s; alcohol twice a month (quantified); accountant; little exercise and frequent takeaway; lives with her husband and dog, with family in town.
check.d: Award for smoking, quantified alcohol, occupation and living situation.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: she wonders whether it is her gallstones, is worried, and wants it sorted.
Examination
Asks for a full set of vital signs and identifies the fever (38.6 °C), tachycardia (112), tachypnoea (22) and soft blood pressure (104/66).
Assesses conscious state and orientation: she gives the wrong day and is slow to answer. Checks for asterixis (absent).
check.d: Critical mark for assessing orientation and conscious state and finding the wrong day and slow responses. Asterixis is optional extra credit.

check.x: Inspects for jaundice, scleral icterus and scratch marks, and assesses hydration (dry mucous membranes, CRT 3 seconds, cool peripheries).
Looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease (clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema, spider naevi, ascites) and for lymphadenopathy, including Virchow's node. All are absent.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Palpates and finds right upper quadrant and epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, and no rigidity.
Checks Murphy's sign (negative), liver size (not enlarged), for a palpable gallbladder (none) and for masses.
kids.d: Credit naming Courvoisier's law when checking for a palpable gallbladder.

check.x: Summarises in Part 1 that jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and fever (Charcot's triad), together with confusion and a soft blood pressure, point to biliary sepsis. States that she needs an ambulance to the ED now, not outpatient tests.
Interpretation

Recognises that she is deteriorating over 75 minutes (SBP 104 to 86, HR 112 to 126, temperature 38.6 to 39.1 °C, RR 22 to 26) with SBP 86 in the red zone (rapid response criteria), and interprets this, with new confusion and lactate 3.6, as sepsis with hypotension and hypoperfusion, at risk of septic shock.
check.d: Optional extra credit: naming HR 126, temperature 39.1 °C and RR 26 as yellow zone values, and defining septic shock as needing vasopressors to keep MAP at or above 65 mmHg, with lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

check.x: Interprets the liver tests as a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern: total bilirubin 98 µmol/L, mostly conjugated (76), with ALP 410 and GGT 520 raised more than ALT 96 and AST 78 (relative to the upper limit of normal: GGT about 15 times and ALP about 3.7 times, ALT about 3 times).
Interprets the other bloods: neutrophilia and CRP 186 show infection; creatinine 118 with no baseline is presumed AKI; normal lipase argues against pancreatitis.

Interprets the ultrasound: the common bile duct is dilated to 11 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal duct and mild intrahepatic duct dilatation. There are gallstones in the gallbladder but no features of cholecystitis.

Gives severe acute cholangitis from common bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis) as the most likely diagnosis. Justifies the severity by Charcot's triad plus confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad), or by organ dysfunction (Tokyo grade III).
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Also credit acute pancreatitis or other reasonable differentials if given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Acute cholecystitis: known gallstones and right upper quadrant pain; against: Murphy's sign negative, no wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and jaundice with a dilated duct.

Primary biliary cholangitis or acute hepatitis: itch with cholestasis, or jaundice with raised transaminases; against: acute febrile illness with a dilated duct and a stone, and no hepatitis risk factors.
Pancreatic head tumour: obstructive jaundice at 56, and the pancreatic head is partly obscured; against: no weight loss or steatorrhoea, a stone is seen, and the onset was acute with fever.

check.x: Interprets the ERCP report: dilated common bile duct with three stones and pus draining from the duct, which confirms cholangitis from choledocholithiasis. Sphincterotomy and balloon extraction cleared the duct, and there is no distal duct stricture or mass effect.
Management

Escalates now: rapid response or senior ED review, and early involvement of the general surgical and gastroenterology teams. Requests ICU review if hypotension persists after fluids (for vasopressors).
Starts sepsis resuscitation within the first hour:

kids.x: Takes two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, without delaying them.
Gives empirical IV antibiotics within 60 minutes as eTG directs (for example piperacillin with tazobactam), noting that she has no drug allergy.
kids.d: Accept any eTG or local biliary sepsis regimen (for example piperacillin with tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly). Credit noting that a single gentamicin dose is acceptable despite the AKI but repeat doses should be avoided or level-guided.

kids.x: Gives an IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL-1 L Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride, up to about 20-30 mL/kg), reassessing after each bolus.
Keeps her nil by mouth, gives IV analgesia and an antiemetic if needed, and stops ibuprofen and other nephrotoxins.
Repeats lactate and places a latex-free urinary catheter for hourly urine output, and flags the latex allergy to ED, endoscopy and theatre.

check.x: Arranges urgent biliary drainage by ERCP once she is resuscitated, because she has severe cholangitis. Percutaneous drainage is the alternative if ERCP fails or is not available.
Plans laparoscopic cholecystectomy once she has recovered, ideally in the same admission or soon after.
check.d: Optional extra credit: completes a short antibiotic course after drainage (at least 2 weeks if blood cultures grow Enterococcus or Streptococcus), tailored to cultures.

check.x: Safety netting
Tells her in plain words when to go to the ED: fever or shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes coming back, dark urine or pale poo, or tummy pain (including while waiting for gallbladder surgery).
check.d: Award for at least two red flags in plain words linked to the ED.

check.x: Tells her to call 000 for confusion, drowsiness, fainting or collapse.
check.d: Award for at least one of these with 000 named.

part2.lead: Your supervising GP called an ambulance, and you went with Michelle to the local emergency department as part of your placement. Here are her observations from the practice and the ED, and her ED blood results and ultrasound. I will give you one more report with the last question.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. The first two sets were taken at the practice; the third at ED triage after the ambulance transfer. No observation chart is used at the practice; the ED uses the NSW adult Between the Flags chart.
handover.model:
• Read: she is getting steadily worse over 75 minutes. Systolic BP has fallen from 104 to 86, HR has risen from 112 to 126, temperature from 38.6 to 39.1 °C and RR from 22 to 26. CRT is now 4 seconds, she is still confused, and the lactate is 3.6. SpO2 is 95% on room air.
  • Zones at ED triage: SBP 86 is in the red zone, so a rapid response call is needed. HR 126, temperature 39.1 °C and RR 26 are in the yellow zone, each of which needs a clinical review. New confusion is a change in conscious state needing at least clinical review and adds to the red-zone call. SpO2 is in the white zone.
  • For Michelle: sepsis with hypotension and hypoperfusion (raised lactate, confusion, slow capillary refill); septic shock if hypotension persists after fluids and needs vasopressors. With jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, this is Reynolds' pentad.
  • What it changes: rapid response and the sepsis pathway now. Cultures, IV antibiotics within the hour, a fluid bolus with reassessment, and ICU review if she stays hypotensive.

rows.note: First set at the practice; new confusion
Repeat set at the practice while waiting for the ambulance; new confusion
ED triage on arrival; new confusion; dizzy sitting up

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Venous blood gas at triage, 11:35; other bloods at 11:40. Venous lactate on the ED blood gas analyser.
handover.model:
• Read: bilirubin 98, mostly conjugated (76). ALP 410 and GGT 520 are raised more than ALT 96 and AST 78 relative to the upper limit of normal (GGT about 15 times, ALP about 3.7 times, ALT about 3 times), which is a cholestatic pattern. WCC 17.8 with neutrophilia and CRP 186. Creatinine 118 with no baseline, so presumed acute kidney injury; the eGFR of 44 is unreliable while creatinine is changing. Urea 9.8. Sodium 134 is mildly low, in keeping with dehydration and sepsis. Lactate 3.6. Haemoglobin, platelets, INR and lipase are normal, and albumin is just low.
  • For Michelle: the conjugated jaundice with a cholestatic pattern points to bile duct obstruction rather than hepatitis or haemolysis. The neutrophilia, CRP and lactate show bacterial sepsis with hypoperfusion. The presumed AKI reflects sepsis and dehydration, made worse by ibuprofen. The normal lipase argues against gallstone pancreatitis.
  • What it changes: her confusion is neurological organ dysfunction, which makes this Tokyo grade III, so drainage is urgent. Creatinine 118 is a presumed AKI but below the TG18 renal threshold (>176.8 µmol/L). Stop ibuprofen; a single empirical gentamicin dose is acceptable despite the AKI, but avoid repeat doses or guide them by levels; monitor urine output.

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, biliary tree, pancreas).

Clinical details: 56-year-old woman with 5 days of jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and fever. Known gallstones. Hypotensive and confused.

Comparison: report of an ultrasound 3 years ago describing gallstones; images not available.

Findings:

  • Gallbladder: multiple mobile calculi, the largest 12 mm. Wall 3 mm (not thickened). No pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic Murphy's sign negative.
  • Common bile duct: dilated to 11 mm. A 9 mm echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing in the distal duct.
  • Intrahepatic ducts: mildly dilated in both lobes.
  • Liver: normal size and echotexture. No focal lesion. Portal vein patent.
  • Pancreas: body and tail normal. The head is partly obscured by bowel gas; no mass seen in the visible parts. No peripancreatic fluid.
  • Other: no free fluid. Spleen and kidneys normal.

Conclusion: dilated common bile duct (11 mm) with a distal duct calculus and mild intrahepatic duct dilatation, consistent with choledocholithiasis. Cholelithiasis without sonographic features of acute cholecystitis. The pancreatic head is incompletely seen.
handover.model:
• Read: dilated common bile duct (11 mm) with a shadowing stone in the distal duct and mild intrahepatic duct dilatation. Gallstones, but a thin gallbladder wall, no pericholecystic fluid and a negative sonographic Murphy's sign. The pancreatic head is only partly seen.
  • For Michelle: a stone obstructing the common bile duct, which explains the obstructive jaundice. With fever and sepsis, this is acute cholangitis. There is no acute cholecystitis.
  • What it changes: ultrasound is the first-line imaging test, and it confirms the obstruction and its cause, so she needs urgent ERCP for drainage and stone extraction. The cholangiogram at ERCP will show whether there is a distal duct stricture; ERCP does not image the pancreatic head itself, so if doubt remains after the duct is cleared, CT, MRCP or EUS can assess it.

handover.label: ERCP report (next morning)
handover.result:
Procedure: endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) under sedation, latex-free precautions.

Clinical details: severe acute cholangitis with sepsis and hypotension; dilated common bile duct with a distal stone on ultrasound. On IV antibiotics.

Findings:

  • Duodenum and papilla: normal papilla in a normal position. Turbid, purulent bile drained after deep biliary cannulation.
  • Cholangiogram: common bile duct dilated to 12 mm with three rounded filling defects in the distal duct, the largest 10 mm, consistent with stones. Mild intrahepatic duct dilatation. No stricture and no mass effect at the distal duct.
  • Therapy: biliary sphincterotomy, then balloon extraction of three stones. The final occlusion cholangiogram showed a clear duct with good drainage. Bile sent for culture.
  • Pancreatic duct: not cannulated.
  • Complications: none. No bleeding after sphincterotomy.

Conclusion: choledocholithiasis with purulent cholangitis. Sphincterotomy and complete stone clearance. Recommend cholecystectomy.
handover.model:
• Read: dilated common bile duct with three filling defects (stones) in the distal duct, and pus from the duct. Sphincterotomy and balloon extraction left a clear duct on the final cholangiogram. No distal duct stricture or mass effect.
  • For Michelle: confirms acute cholangitis from choledocholithiasis. The source is drained, and no malignant stricture is seen.
  • What it changes: expect her to improve clinically and her LFTs to fall. Tailor the antibiotics to the blood and bile cultures, with a short course now that the source is controlled (at least 2 weeks if blood cultures grow Enterococcus or Streptococcus). Watch for post-ERCP pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation. She still has gallstones, so she needs a cholecystectomy once she has recovered, ideally in the same admission or soon after, to prevent more stones passing.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar from the emergency department. Please give an ISBAR handover of Michelle Stark, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Michelle now, here in the emergency department.
Here is the ERCP report from the next morning. What does it show, and what red flags will you give Michelle before discharge?
expect:
• Identify: self (fourth-year medical student, ED); Michelle Stark, 56.
  • Situation: severe acute cholangitis with sepsis, hypotension and raised lactate; needs surgical review and urgent biliary drainage.
  • Background: 5 days of jaundice, RUQ pain, fever and new confusion; untreated gallstones; ibuprofen; latex allergy, no drug allergy.
  • Assessment: BP 86/50 (red zone), HR 126, T 39.1, RR 26, confused, lactate 3.6, deteriorating; obstructive LFTs; WCC 17.8; presumed AKI; US CBD 11 mm with distal stone.
  • Recommendation: Please review now. I am starting cultures, IV antibiotics within the hour and a fluid bolus with the ED team; she needs urgent ERCP once resuscitated, and ICU if still hypotensive.

Most likely: severe acute cholangitis from common bile duct stones. She has Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever), and with confusion and hypotension this is Reynolds' pentad. Known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern, and a dilated duct with a stone on ultrasound.

  • Acute cholecystitis: for: gallstones, right upper quadrant pain. Against: Murphy's negative, no wall thickening, jaundice with a dilated duct.
  • Primary biliary cholangitis: for: middle-aged woman with itch and cholestasis. Against: acute, febrile, dilated duct with a stone.
  • Acute hepatitis: for: raised ALT. Against: no risk factors, cholestatic pattern.
  • Pancreatic head tumour: for: obstructive jaundice, head partly obscured. Against: no weight loss, acute febrile onset, stone seen.

1. Escalate now: rapid response or ED senior; involve surgery and gastroenterology early; ICU if hypotension persists after fluids (vasopressors).
  2. Sepsis pathway in the first hour: two sets of blood cultures, then IV antibiotics within 60 minutes as eTG directs (for example piperacillin with tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly). A single gentamicin dose is acceptable despite the AKI; avoid repeat doses or guide them by levels.
  3. Fluids: IV crystalloid bolus (for example 500 mL to 1 L of Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride, up to about 20 to 30 mL/kg), reassessing after each bolus. Repeat lactate; latex-free urinary catheter for hourly urine output; flag the latex allergy to ED, endoscopy and theatre.
  4. Supportive care: nil by mouth, IV analgesia, an antiemetic if needed, stop ibuprofen.
  5. Source control: urgent ERCP once resuscitated (percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails).
  6. Definitive: laparoscopic cholecystectomy once recovered, ideally in the same admission.

• ERCP: dilated common bile duct, three distal stones and pus, which confirms cholangitis from choledocholithiasis; duct cleared after sphincterotomy; no stricture or mass.
  • Red flags: go to the ED for fever or shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes again, dark urine or pale poo, or tummy pain; call 000 for confusion, drowsiness or collapse.

ddx.dx: Severe acute cholangitis due to choledocholithiasis, with sepsis and hypotension (at risk of septic shock)
ddx.for: Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension with known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern and a dilated duct with a distal stone.
Known gallstones with right upper quadrant pain, fever and a neutrophilia.
ddx.against: Murphy's sign negative, no gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and conjugated jaundice with a dilated common bile duct.

ddx.for: A middle-aged woman with itch and a cholestatic LFT pattern.
ddx.against: Acute 5-day febrile illness with sepsis, and a dilated duct with a stone on ultrasound.

ddx.for: Jaundice with raised ALT and AST.
ddx.against: No risk factors, travel or contacts, ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases, and a dilated duct.

ddx.dx: Pancreatic head carcinoma causing malignant biliary obstruction
ddx.for: Obstructive jaundice at 56, and the pancreatic head was partly obscured on ultrasound.
ddx.against: No weight loss or steatorrhoea, acute febrile onset, a stone seen in the duct, and no distal duct stricture or mass effect on the ERCP cholangiogram.

ddx.for: Gallstones with upper abdominal pain and a stone in the distal common bile duct.
ddx.against: Normal lipase and no peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart in Part 1: give the 10:20 observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. Give other findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for blood tests or imaging in Part 1, say they will come in Part 2. If they decide she needs hospital, say the supervising GP agrees and is calling an ambulance. Credit this decision in Part 1. The confusion is only revealed when the candidate asks about it (or asks an open question about other symptoms); Michelle doesn't volunteer it.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods and ultrasound, then ask the first three questions in order. Hand over the ERCP report with the fourth question. The observation rows are what happened whatever the candidate did, and they record no treatment.

The source case asks which initial imaging to order and gives ERCP as the answer. In current practice, ultrasound is the first imaging test and urgent ERCP is used to drain the duct. Credit a candidate who says that ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic in Charcot's triad with abnormal LFTs, as long as resuscitation and antibiotics come first.

A high-performing candidate characterises the jaundice and pain and asks the 4 Ps. They draw out the fever, dizziness and confusion, ask about symptoms of at least three other causes, and find the known gallstones, the ibuprofen and the latex allergy. They check her orientation, examine the abdomen, and recognise in Part 1 that she is septic and needs the ED now. In Part 2 they see that she is deteriorating, with sepsis, hypotension and a raised lactate, and is at risk of septic shock. They read the cholestatic pattern and the ultrasound correctly, name severe cholangitis, and start the sepsis bundle within the hour, with urgent ERCP, escalation and a cholecystectomy plan.

A borderline candidate takes a generic jaundice history and misses the confusion or the falling blood pressure. They may plan outpatient tests or an ultrasound before antibiotics, or call it cholecystitis or hepatitis. They may also forget the latex allergy, or leave her on ibuprofen.
explain:
Diagnosis

Michelle has severe acute cholangitis: bacterial infection of an obstructed common bile duct, here caused by stones (choledocholithiasis) passed from a gallbladder full of gallstones that had never been treated. She has Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and fever). She also has confusion and, by the time she reaches the ED, hypotension. Together these make Reynolds' pentad, which marks sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypoperfusion and needs urgent drainage of the duct. Her dizziness was an early sign of hypotension. The confusion is easy to miss because she mentioned it only as a co-worker's comment.

Classifying jaundice

  • Unconjugated: too much bilirubin is made (haemolysis), or the liver takes up too little (for example rifampicin) or conjugates too little (Gilbert's syndrome).
  • Mixed or conjugated: impaired secretion or intrahepatic cholestasis (for example drug-induced cholestasis, primary biliary cholangitis), hepatocellular injury (hepatitis), or bile duct obstruction (choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head tumour).

In a jaundice history, ask about the 4 Ps: pee (dark urine), poo (pale stools), pruritus and pain. Also ask about viral hepatitis risk factors, alcohol and medicines. Pale stools, itch and pain point to obstruction. Then ask about each differential: pain after meals or rigors (gallstone disease), risk factors and malaise (hepatitis), weight loss and steatorrhoea (pancreatic cancer), and previous episodes or anaemia (haemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome).

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: her blood pressure fell and her heart rate, temperature and respiratory rate rose over 75 minutes. At ED triage, SBP 86 is in the red zone of the NSW Between the Flags chart (rapid response); HR, temperature and RR are in the yellow zone. With confusion and a lactate of 3.6, this is sepsis with hypotension and hypoperfusion. Under the Sepsis-3 definition used by the ACSQHC and eTG, it becomes septic shock only if she still needs vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg, with lactate >2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
  • LFTs: a cholestatic pattern, with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT and AST and a mostly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, points to obstruction. A transaminase rise is common in acute duct obstruction. In the Tokyo Guidelines 2018, bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL (about 85 µmol/L), WCC >12 × 109/L and temperature ≥39 °C are grade II features. Confusion is neurological organ dysfunction, which makes it grade III (severe). Hypotension would also count if vasopressors are needed.
  • Other bloods: the neutrophilia and CRP show infection and the lactate shows hypoperfusion. The AKI comes from sepsis, dehydration and ibuprofen; creatinine 118 is below the Tokyo renal dysfunction threshold (>176.8 µmol/L). A normal haemoglobin argues against haemolysis and a normal lipase against pancreatitis.
  • Ultrasound: a dilated common bile duct with a distal stone, with no features of cholecystitis.
  • ERCP: stones in the common bile duct with purulent bile. The duct was cleared after sphincterotomy.

Imaging

The source case answers ERCP as the first imaging test, because with Charcot's triad and abnormal LFTs, ERCP both confirms the stones and drains the duct. In practice, ultrasound is the first-line test: it is quick, safe, and shows duct dilatation and stones. ERCP is reserved for drainage, because it carries risks of pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation. If the ultrasound is normal but suspicion remains, CT (or MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound) is the next step. Imaging never delays cultures, antibiotics and resuscitation.

Management

  • Recognise and escalate: a red zone observation means a rapid response call (NSW Health deteriorating patient policy). Involve the surgical and gastroenterology teams early, and ICU if hypotension persists after fluids.
  • Sepsis care (ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard): blood cultures, then empirical IV antibiotics within 60 minutes. Use an eTG biliary sepsis regimen (for example piperacillin with tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly). A single empirical gentamicin dose is acceptable despite the AKI, but repeat doses should be avoided or guided by levels. Adjust to the cultures. Give an IV crystalloid bolus (for example 500 mL to 1 L of Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride, up to about 20 to 30 mL/kg), reassessing after each bolus, and monitor lactate and urine output.
  • Supportive care: nil by mouth, IV analgesia and an antiemetic if needed. Stop ibuprofen. Use latex-free equipment, including the urinary catheter.
  • Source control: severe cholangitis needs urgent biliary drainage as soon as she is resuscitated, usually by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (or a stent). Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the alternative when ERCP fails or is not available. Once the duct is drained, antibiotics usually continue for a short course of about 4 to 7 days (at least 2 weeks if blood cultures grow Enterococcus or Streptococcus) (Tokyo Guidelines 2018).
  • Definitive treatment: laparoscopic cholecystectomy once she has recovered, ideally during the same admission or soon after, because stones left in the gallbladder will cause further cholangitis, pancreatitis or cholecystitis. After grade III cholangitis, surgery is often deferred until the organ dysfunction has resolved.

Safety netting

Before discharge, tell her to go to the ED for fever or shaking chills, yellow skin or eyes again, dark urine or pale stools, or abdominal pain, especially while she waits for surgery. Tell her to call 000 for confusion, drowsiness or collapse. Arrange GP review with repeat LFTs and kidney function, avoid NSAIDs until the kidney function has recovered, and confirm the surgical plan.

Follow-up after discharge

A surgical clinic appointment for cholecystectomy if it was not done in hospital, and GP review in 1 to 2 weeks with repeat LFTs and kidney function. Confirm the antibiotic course is complete, and no ibuprofen until kidney function is rechecked.
points: Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever) suggests acute cholangitis. Adding confusion and hypotension makes Reynolds' pentad, which marks sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypoperfusion and needs urgent drainage of the bile duct.
In every jaundice history, ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain), viral hepatitis risk factors, alcohol and medicines, and ask specifically about confusion, which patients may not volunteer.
A cholestatic pattern (ALP and GGT raised more than ALT and AST, with conjugated bilirubin) points to biliary obstruction; ultrasound is the first-line imaging test to show a dilated duct and stones.
Treat suspected cholangitis as sepsis: blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 60 minutes, fluids and early escalation, then urgent ERCP for source control once she is resuscitated.
After cholangitis from common bile duct stones, the gallbladder still holds stones, so plan cholecystectomy once she has recovered, ideally in the same admission or soon after.
Check for latex allergy and stop NSAIDs in a septic patient with acute kidney injury.
